[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: English 'if' (and 'whenever') states a standing rule that stays in force and fires whenever its condition becomes true. A Java if is evaluated once, when control reaches it, and then is 'taken off the books'; changing the variables later does not re-trigger it.
[1] misconception (M) -> IfIsLoop: wrong rule: an if body repeats while its condition holds. Right rule: An if body runs at most once; only a loop repeats its body.
[2] misconception (M) -> IfRequiresElse: wrong rule: Every if statement requires an else. Right rule: An if statement may stand alone; the else part is optional.
[3] misconception (M) -> FalseConditionEndsProgram: wrong rule: A false condition with no else ends the program. Right rule: When an if condition is false and there is no else, execution continues with the statement after the if.
[4] misconception (M) -> ThenAlwaysExecutes: wrong rule: The then branch always runs. Right rule: The then branch runs only when the condition is true.
[5] misconception (M) -> CodeAfterIfSkipped: wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. Right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.
[6] misconception (M) -> NextStatementIsElse: wrong rule: In if (c) A; B; the statement B runs only when c is false. Right rule: B is not part of the if; it runs every time.
[7] misconception (M) -> IfWaitsForCondition: wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. Right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.
[8] misconception (M) -> BranchChosenByIntent: wrong rule: Which branch runs is decided by what the programmer meant or by code outside the if, not by whether the condition is true. Right rule: The then branch runs exactly when the condition evaluates to true at the moment it is tested; otherwise the else branch (if any) runs.
[9] misconception (M) -> StatementAfterIfInBranch: wrong rule: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true. Right rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.
[10] misconception (M) -> FalseConditionRestartsProgram: wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. Right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.
[11] misconception (M) -> IfConditionWatched: wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). Right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.
[12] misconception (M) -> IfConditionCheckedInHindsight: wrong rule: Whether the branch runs is decided by the condition after the branch, or from the point inside the body where the condition becomes true. Right rule: The condition is tested once, before the branch; the whole branch runs if it was true at that moment and none of it runs otherwise.
[13] misconception (M) -> IfInLoopUnchecked: wrong rule: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition. Right rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true.
[14] inconsistent_trace (T) -> IfIsLoop: Applies the if rule (LT) unevenly: tests the condition on some visits but not others (e.g. runs the branch on every loop pass without testing), runs the branch after a false test, or re-checks the condition after the branch has run. (here mixing in: "an if body repeats while its condition holds")
[15] misconception (M) -> AssignCompares: wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
[16] misconception (M) -> LoopForOneTimeTest: wrong rule: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once. Right rule: A test made once is an if; a loop repeats.
[17] misconception (M) -> MapToBooleanWithIf: wrong rule: you need an if to turn a boolean expression into a boolean. Right rule: ok = (x > y); stores the result of the comparison directly.
[18] misconception (M) -> ProgramLooksAhead: wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
[19] misconception (M) -> SequentialIfsAreNested: wrong rule: Of two if statements one after the other, the second runs its body only if both conditions are true. Right rule: Two ifs in sequence are independent: each tests only its own condition.

[0] names_the_element (N): The if statement is a conditional (selection) statement: it runs a statement or block only when a boolean condition is true.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Syntax: if (<boolean expression>) <statement or { block }>; the braces are optional when the body is a single statement. The expression must have type boolean (or Boolean), and the body is executed if and only if the expression is true.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Evaluate the condition once; if true, execute the body; then, in either case, continue with the statement after the if.
[1] output_prediction (OP): An if produces no value; its observable result is that the body's effects (assignments, output) happen exactly once when the condition is true and not at all when it is false; e.g. if (x < 0) x = -x; leaves x = 5 for 5 and gives 5 for -5.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One execution reads the variables in the condition, changes nothing by the test itself (unless the condition has a side effect), and, when true, applies the body's changes once; control then moves to the next statement.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The condition must be a boolean expression; a non-boolean condition such as if (t = goal) with int t is a compile-time error, while if (b = false) with boolean b compiles and assigns.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): if-else extends if with a second branch that runs exactly when the condition is false; a lone if has an implicit empty else-case.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): An if is a fork in the control flow: one path through the body, one around it, both rejoining at the next statement.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): if and while have the same form, but if tests its condition once and runs the block at most once, while while tests again after every pass and repeats the block as long as the condition is true.
[4] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: guard / conditional action - do something only for the inputs that need it (absolute value, put two values in order, error check before dividing).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> IfIsLoop: Negating the condition swaps which inputs run the body; changing < to <= changes only the boundary value. Adding a statement under a braceless if does not put it in the body. Whatever the condition, code after the if still runs exactly once.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A ; right after if (...) is an empty statement that forms the whole then branch; the following statement or block is no longer part of the if. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Any if (cond); followed by a statement or block: that statement runs for every input, whatever cond is (it compiles without error).
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The if template is if (<boolean expression>) <statement>: the condition must be enclosed in parentheses. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Any if whose condition is written in { } or without ( ), e.g. if {x > 0} ... or if a > b { c = 0; }.
[3] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use an if when an action is needed for some inputs only and the test happens once at that point; use a loop if the action must repeat while the condition holds, and assign a boolean directly (ok = x > y;) when you only need the truth value.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Without braces, the body of an if, while or for is exactly one statement; indentation does not add statements to it. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A braceless header followed by two or more indented statements: only the first is controlled, the others run once, after the if/loop, on every input.
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The condition of an if must have type boolean. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Using = instead of == with int operands, e.g. if (t = goal): 'incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean'.
[6] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: With boolean operands, = is assignment, not comparison. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: if (isPrime = false) with boolean isPrime: compiles, sets isPrime to false and the branch never runs.

if and while have the same form, but if tests its condition once and runs the block at most once, while while tests again after every pass and repeats the block as long as the condition is true.
An if runs its block only when its boolean expression evaluates to true.
An if changes the default top-to-bottom flow by running a block only when its condition is true.
if-else extends if with a second block that runs exactly when the condition is false.
An if statement can sit inside the body of another if; the inner one is tested only when the outer condition is true.
